questions.stem: Which of the following is a physical change?

options.text: Rusting of an iron roofing sheet

questions.explanation: Melting wax only changes the state of the wax; cooling it solidifies the same substance again, so no new substance is formed. The other three all produce new substances with different chemical properties.

distractorRationale.a: Rusting forms hydrated iron(III) oxide, a new compound that cannot be turned back into iron by cooling
distractorRationale.c: Souring produces lactic acid from lactose, a new substance
distractorRationale.d: Burning charcoal converts carbon into carbon dioxide with a large release of heat

questions.stem: Which of the following is a compound?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide contains carbon and oxygen chemically combined in the fixed ratio of one carbon atom to two oxygen atoms, and it can only be split apart by chemical means. That fixed composition is what defines a compound.

distractorRationale.a: Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen and other gases in variable proportions
distractorRationale.b: Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc, that is an alloy, whose composition can be varied
distractorRationale.d: Sulphur is an element made of only one kind of atom

questions.stem: A property that distinguishes a mixture from a compound is that a mixture

options.text: always contains only one kind of atom
has a sharp, constant melting point
can be separated into its components by physical methods
is always formed with a large release of heat

questions.explanation: In a mixture the components are only physically intermingled, so differences in properties such as boiling point, solubility or magnetism can be exploited to separate them. A compound is held together by chemical bonds and can only be broken up chemically.

distractorRationale.a: That describes an element, not a mixture
distractorRationale.b: A sharp melting point is a sign of a pure substance; mixtures melt over a range
distractorRationale.d: A definite energy change accompanies compound formation, not the making of a mixture

questions.stem: A grey powder is stirred with a yellow powder. A magnet removes the grey solid completely. The remaining yellow solid dissolves in carbon disulphide. The original sample was

options.text: a mixture of iron and sulphur
a solution of sulphur in iron

questions.explanation: Both components kept their individual properties: the iron was still magnetic and the sulphur still dissolved in carbon disulphide. Physical methods separated them completely, which is the defining behaviour of a mixture.

distractorRationale.a: Iron(II) sulphide is black, non-magnetic and insoluble in carbon disulphide because the elements have lost their separate identities
distractorRationale.c: An element contains only one kind of atom and cannot be split into two different solids
distractorRationale.d: A solution is homogeneous, whereas the two powders remained visibly distinct

questions.stem: Blue copper(II) sulphate crystals are heated gently in a test tube. A white solid remains and droplets collect at the cooler end. Adding the droplets back to the white solid restores the blue colour. This change is best described as

options.text: physical, because no new substance is formed at any stage
chemical, because a new substance is formed and the change involves breaking bonds to water of crystallisation
physical, because the colour change is only temporary
neither physical nor chemical, because the mass does not change

questions.explanation: Heating drives off water of crystallisation, converting hydrated CuSO4.5H2O into anhydrous CuSO4. A genuinely new substance with different colour and formula is produced, so the change is chemical. The fact that it can be reversed does not make it physical, since many chemical changes are reversible.

distractorRationale.a: Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate is a different compound from the hydrated form
distractorRationale.c: Reversibility is a weak clue; the deciding test is whether a new substance with a new formula exists
distractorRationale.d: Mass is conserved in every change, so it cannot be used to classify one

questions.stem: Which statement about elements is correct?

options.text: An element can be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means
An element contains only one kind of atom
Every element exists as single unbonded atoms
Elements always have a fixed ratio of two different atoms

questions.explanation: An element is a substance made up of atoms that all have the same atomic number, that is the same number of protons. That is why no chemical reaction can decompose it into anything simpler.

distractorRationale.a: This is the opposite of the definition; only compounds decompose chemically
distractorRationale.c: Many elements exist as molecules, such as O2, N2, Cl2 and S8, yet they are still elements
distractorRationale.d: A fixed ratio of two different atoms describes a compound

questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates a chemical change?

options.text: Iron rusting in the presence of oxygen

questions.explanation: Iron rusting involves a reaction with oxygen to form iron oxide, which is a new substance. In contrast, melting ice or dissolving sugar are physical changes where the original substances remain unchanged.

distractorRationale.a: Melting ice is a physical change where the state of water changes but its chemical composition remains the same.
distractorRationale.c: Dissolving sugar in water is a physical change; the sugar can be recovered by evaporation.
distractorRationale.d: Chopping wood is a physical change as the wood's composition remains unchanged.

questions.stem: When a candle burns, which of the following occurs?

options.text: The wax melts and can be reused
The wax is converted into carbon dioxide and water

distractorRationale.c: The wick does burn and changes chemically, so it does not remain the same.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly describes a characteristic of compounds?

Compounds have properties different from their constituent elements

questions.explanation: Compounds are formed when elements chemically combine, resulting in new properties that differ from those of the individual elements. This is a fundamental characteristic of compounds.
